author: hoeschec
text:
Thanks Jurij

I've gotten better managing my emotions when it comes to trading, but I gotta admit EUR-AUD had smoke coming from my ears yesterday

Juri, you hit the 'nail on the head' when you wrote " If so, there must be a way to know which level the ITs are targetting for the final reversal? Or are we supposed to guess the level by taking a few losses on the way? There's always a better level above/below."

I don't know the answer to this, but here is something I've been pondering for quite some time now.

I look at many successful trades where price reacts exactly as I predict, and my target is hit. Even in these trades, there are MPL's that haven't been hit above my entry. There is always a better level above/below an entry. We can't put a 500+ pip stop on every trade to account for the possibility that price will do some crap like this.

What I am coming to believe: The market is reasonably easy to predict if you have the right understanding of why price moves from level to level. I must admit, as unpopular as this viewpoint may be, I don't believe anyone can predict the market 100% of the time...even 90% of time. There are too many external factors that contribute to the global markets to say that there is a secret that will give us 90+ success rate in taking trades.

What I think RTM does best is teach a method to analyze the market in a way the cracks the code on how the algorithms work on the super computers that trade most of the IT's capital. The algorithms are predictable because they operate consistently...until they are adjusted/changed. There are so many big players in the market, sometimes an infusion of orders will enter the market and blow through setups that worked in the past. I don't think it is always our fault (sometimes it is) but it may be worth accepting there will be losses...our success depends on how we handle our losses. I don't think we spend enough time taking about this on RTM and it needs to change. All traders lose...and they lose on a regular basis. It his how they handle the losses that determines whether they are successful.

I do believe there is chaos (at times) in the market. There is unpredictability (at times) in the market. That is OK...we shouldn't try to over analyze why every trade goes against us. It is important to autopsy every loss to determine if there was a mistake in the analysis (this is critical) but it's OK to come to the conclusion that the trade failed...there isn't always a reason.

Once we can free ourselves from internalizing every loss as 'our fault' we can move past the losses and re focus our efforts on the next setup.

EUR-AUD is a good example...I should have been out after the ten pip loss. Instead I got back in and tried to get the next open level of FOF...which got blown through again and again and again. The trade I took yesterday has worked in the past (with regard to my analysis and execution). This time something else occurred, I was wrong, and that is OK.

If the market stops out a position, I need to accept it and move on. Tight stops, wide targets. Emotionless trading.

If I could sum up RTM and its concepts in a simple way I would say: RTM doesn't contain a special secret or 'holy grail' of trading. It teaches you to understand the market in such a way that you can get in to the market with very limited risk and very wide targets. In my opinion, this is the inherent beauty of the RTM forum and the education here. We trade at the best moments when FOF is likely to exist and reverse price.

It doesn't mean we are right all the time...and that is OK. I think it is a waste of time trying to be right 100% of the time. It is impossible.

With the right application and through hard work, RTM teaches a method of understanding PA in a way that ensures you will still be wildly successful...even if you are wrong half the time

Just my opinion, and I hope I didn't offend anyone!

author: hoeschec
text:
"If the signal is given by the market mover (an engulf into a new zone), then price is very unlikely to break the extreme of the zone it just came from. So, if you have the patience to wait at the last remaining set of unfilled orders in the origin, you can be almost certain that that price will be respected." - IF

We have seen multiple examples this week of price engulfing and faking out very high above the engulf....much higher than the origin of the engulf. Is IF's statement above still accurate or has the market changed since he wrote this? I know there have been some changes to the algorithms in the past year that make FO more severe.

Can anyone show this concept on a real chart?

I thought I understood the concept but what does IF mean by 'zone'? And how is the zone different from an origin? Every engulf and RT/FTR forms a new origin. There are origins everywhere within the different scales. What does IF mean by 'zone' and how do we draw these zones, and what is the the 'extreme' of a zone? Is he referring to the MPL?

This also would help answer Jurij's question back on Post #1357 when he says (with regard to a valid engulf occurring) "If so, there must be a way to know which level the ITs are targeting for the final reversal? Or are we supposed to guess the level by taking a few losses on the way?

Thanks

Another one: If we've had an engulf and are getting in on a RT, we must always be ready for a diamond to occur, especially if price hasn't yet hit MPL of the zone the original bounce was a reaction to. So, if we're not going to be around to watch PA, our stop must be beyond the original FL. - IF

author: hoeschec
text:
I don't really understand the PAZ concept. What makes a PAZ so important? Isn't it just space between FTR/FL? It is the FTR/FL that matters because it is where the FOF exists.

Without scale, the PAZ is not useful. Without scale, nothing we learn here is useful because there is always a multitude of reasons why a trade can go wrong. It just doesn't make sense to me.

Unless you know with relative certainty that price will stop at a certain FL, you really have no way of knowing if your trade will be successful. There is always another area that price can FO to for a better price. Are we supposed to guess which level price will stop at? I don't think that is how the advanced traders on RTM do it...they seem to know the absolute best location to get in a trade.

For as many winning trades as I've posted recently, I have also lost many trades.

Understanding how the PAZ interacts with scale to give us an MPL that fits within the correct scale is critical. Does anyone have advice on journals I can read through to find this information? I find very, very little on this topic. Seeing successful trades posted is helpful to some degree, but without a real explanation we are limited in our progress as traders.

Again, I go back to this quote from IF:

"If the signal is given by the market mover (an engulf into a new zone), then price is very unlikely to break the extreme of the zone it just came from. So, if you have the patience to wait at the last remaining set of unfilled orders in the origin, you can be almost certain that that price will be respected." - IF

Where can I go, and what can I read to understand what he is talking about here? If zone = PAZ, then where can I learn to combine the issue of scale with the concept of a PAZ?

If a PAZ is the area between two FTR's, then on every single scale there will be multiple PAZ. If we wait for an engulf of an important level, and want to get in at the most extreme zone with remaining FOF, how do we choose the zone/PAZ that will ultimately bounce price?

Thanks
